title: 1 Chronicles 2:1–17
context: Chapter 2 names the sons of Israel, then concentrates on Judah, from the sons born to him down to Jesse, David, and the children of Zeruiah and Abigail. The twelve sons in 2:1–2 follow the familiar list of Jacob’s sons, known from Genesis (for example Genesis 35:23–26 and 46:8–25), though the order here is not identical with every Genesis listing and should not be forced into one official sequence. Judah’s first sons, and Tamar’s bearing of Perez and Zerah, parallel Genesis 38. Perez’s line through Hezron, Ram, Amminadab, Nahshon, Salma, Boaz, Obed, and Jesse to David parallels Ruth 4:18–22, where Nahshon’s son is Salmon, not Salma, a spelling difference to be named, not explained away. The already drafted Ruth 4 notes treat that genealogy as a real line that may also be selective in its generations; the same caution belongs here. In 2:6 Zerah’s sons are five, including Dara; in 2:7 Carmi’s son is Achar, “the troubler of Israel, who committed a trespass in the devoted thing” a record commonly set beside Achan in Joshua 7, with a different spelling, without a required identification beyond what the two texts allow. Jesse’s sons are listed through “David the seventh” while 1 Samuel 16–17 presents David among Jesse’s sons in a way that has often been counted differently; the difference should be named, not harmonized. The unit closes with David’s sisters Zeruiah and Abigail and their sons, including Joab, Abishai, Asahel, and Amasa, figures already met in Samuel. Both traditions take the Chronicler to be tracing the royal line through Judah, inside Israel’s own families.

verses.text: These are the sons of Israel: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun,
verses.arminianNotes:
“These are the sons of Israel: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun,” The list continues in the next verse. The twelve will be complete there. The names are those of Jacob’s sons in Genesis, though the order of the tribes is not the same in every Genesis list and should not be forced into one sequence.

Arminian readers hear a historical household, Israel’s own sons, now at the center of the book.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the Chronicler turning from Abraham’s wider family to Israel’s twelve, a real narrowing toward Judah and the royal line.

Both traditions read this stretch as the Chronicler turning from the world’s families to Israel, and then narrowing toward Judah’s royal line, without allegory and without forcing the parallel lists into one form.

verses.text: Dan, Joseph, Benjamin, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher.
verses.arminianNotes:
The twelve are completed: “Dan, Joseph, Benjamin, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher.” With verse 1, all the sons of Israel are named. The following verses will not treat each tribe; they will follow Judah.

Arminian readers take the finished twelve as a genuine family register, then watch the Chronicler choose the line that leads to David.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise read the close of the twelve as the book’s way of locating Judah inside Israel before the royal genealogy begins.

Both traditions read this stretch as the Chronicler turning from the world’s families to Israel, and then narrowing toward Judah’s royal line, without allegory and without forcing the parallel lists into one form.

verses.text: The sons of Judah: Er, Onan, and Shelah, which three were born to him of Shua’s daughter the Canaanitess. Er, Judah’s firstborn, was wicked in the LORD’s sight; and he killed him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Judah’s first three sons, Er, Onan, and Shelah, were born of Shua’s daughter the Canaanitess. “Er, Judah’s firstborn, was wicked in the LORD’s sight; and he killed him.” The notice parallels Genesis 38, where Er and Onan die and Shelah remains. The Chronicler records the judgment without retelling the whole chapter.

Arminian readers take the moral fact as it is given: Er was wicked in the LORD’s sight, and the LORD killed him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same Genesis 38 parallel, stated briefly. The royal tribe’s line begins with a judgment, not with a cleaned list.

Both traditions read this stretch as the Chronicler turning from the world’s families to Israel, and then narrowing toward Judah’s royal line, without allegory and without forcing the parallel lists into one form.

verses.text: Tamar his daughter-in-law bore him Perez and Zerah. All the sons of Judah were five.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Tamar his daughter-in-law bore him Perez and Zerah. All the sons of Judah were five.” The verse assumes the story of Genesis 38 without repeating it, and then counts Judah’s sons as five: the three of verse 3 and the two born to Tamar.

Arminian readers keep Tamar’s place in the line as the text gives it, a real birth by a daughter-in-law, not a scene to be turned into allegory here.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also name Genesis 38 as the parallel and accept the count of five. Perez, who will carry the line toward David, is introduced beside Zerah.

Both traditions read this stretch as the Chronicler turning from the world’s families to Israel, and then narrowing toward Judah’s royal line, without allegory and without forcing the parallel lists into one form.

verses.text: The sons of Perez: Hezron and Hamul.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The sons of Perez: Hezron and Hamul.” The same two sons stand in Genesis 46:12 and in the opening of the Perez line in Ruth 4:18. The royal genealogy will run through Hezron.

Arminian readers take Hezron and Hamul as historical sons of Perez, the next step in a real family record.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same names as Ruth 4:18 and Genesis 46:12. From Hezron the Chronicler will move, in the next verses, toward David.

Both traditions read this stretch as the Chronicler turning from the world’s families to Israel, and then narrowing toward Judah’s royal line, without allegory and without forcing the parallel lists into one form.

verses.text: The sons of Zerah: Zimri, Ethan, Heman, Calcol, and Dara—five of them in all.
verses.arminianNotes:
Zerah’s sons are Zimri, Ethan, Heman, Calcol, and Dara, “five of them in all.” The verse is a side-branch of Judah, not the line that will run through Perez to David. Other lists in Scripture sometimes show similar names with different spellings; such comparisons should be named only with care and not forced.

Arminian readers keep the five as Zerah’s sons in this book, a genuine branch, not a riddle.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also refuse to build doctrine or a harmony on possible name-overlaps. The Chronicler records five sons of Zerah and then returns toward Hezron’s line.

Both traditions read this stretch as the Chronicler turning from the world’s families to Israel, and then narrowing toward Judah’s royal line, without allegory and without forcing the parallel lists into one form.

verses.text: The son of Carmi: Achar, the troubler of Israel, who committed a trespass in the devoted thing.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The son of Carmi: Achar, the troubler of Israel, who committed a trespass in the devoted thing.” The wording explains the name by the deed. Readers commonly set this verse beside Achan in Joshua 7, where a trespass in the devoted thing is told at length, with a different spelling of the name. The parallel should be named; the spellings should not be forced into one form as if the texts had no difference.

Arminian readers take the notice as a real remembered offense in Judah’s family.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise point to Joshua 7 without declaring a single official spelling. The Chronicler includes the troubler in the genealogy, not only the royal names.

Both traditions read this stretch as the Chronicler turning from the world’s families to Israel, and then narrowing toward Judah’s royal line, without allegory and without forcing the parallel lists into one form.

verses.arminianNotes:
“The son of Ethan: Azariah.” The verse is a brief continuation of Zerah’s branch from verse 6, where Ethan was named. No further story is given here.

Arminian readers let a single name stand as a historical note, without inventing a life or a type for this Azariah.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also decline to identify this Azariah with later men of the same name unless the text itself does so. The list is still in Judah, still a family record.

Both traditions read this stretch as the Chronicler turning from the world’s families to Israel, and then narrowing toward Judah’s royal line, without allegory and without forcing the parallel lists into one form.

verses.text: The sons also of Hezron, who were born to him: Jerahmeel, Ram, and Chelubai.
verses.arminianNotes:
Hezron’s sons, born to him, are Jerahmeel, Ram, and Chelubai. Ram will carry the line toward David in the next verses; Jerahmeel and Chelubai (often discussed in connection with Caleb later in the chapter) will be taken up afterward. Those later identifications should be hedged, not assumed in this verse.

Arminian readers take the three as Hezron’s real sons, the fork from which several Judahite lines will run.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same fork. Ruth 4:19 follows Ram; this book will follow him first, then return to the brothers, without forcing all the names into one person.

Both traditions read this stretch as the Chronicler turning from the world’s families to Israel, and then narrowing toward Judah’s royal line, without allegory and without forcing the parallel lists into one form.

verses.text: Ram became the father of Amminadab, and Amminadab became the father of Nahshon, prince of the children of Judah;
verses.arminianNotes:
“Ram became the father of Amminadab, and Amminadab became the father of Nahshon, prince of the children of Judah;” The same descent stands in Ruth 4:19–20, where Nahshon is also named, and the already drafted Ruth notes recall his place in Judah. Here he is called prince of the children of Judah.

Arminian readers take the titles and the births as historical links in the line toward David.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers read a close parallel to Ruth 4:19–20, with the added notice that Nahshon was prince of Judah. The royal line is being traced, step by step.

Both traditions read this stretch as the Chronicler turning from the world’s families to Israel, and then narrowing toward Judah’s royal line, without allegory and without forcing the parallel lists into one form.

verses.text: and Nahshon became the father of Salma, and Salma became the father of Boaz,
verses.arminianNotes:
“and Nahshon became the father of Salma, and Salma became the father of Boaz,” Ruth 4:20–21 has Salmon, not Salma, as Nahshon’s son and Boaz’s father. The spelling differs and should be reported as a difference, not explained away.

Arminian readers can name Salma and Salmon together as the two lists give them, and still follow the line to Boaz.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave Salma and Salmon as a variant between 2:11 and Ruth 4:20–21. The Chronicler is still tracing the same descent toward Jesse and David.

Both traditions read this stretch as the Chronicler turning from the world’s families to Israel, and then narrowing toward Judah’s royal line, without allegory and without forcing the parallel lists into one form.

verses.text: and Boaz became the father of Obed, and Obed became the father of Jesse;
verses.arminianNotes:
“and Boaz became the father of Obed, and Obed became the father of Jesse;” The two steps match Ruth 4:21–22. The story of Ruth is not retold; the names are kept in the royal list.

Arminian readers hear the same historical close of that short genealogy, now set inside Chronicles’ larger Judahite record.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the verse as the same link as Ruth 4:21–22, Boaz and Obed leading to Jesse, on the way to David.

Both traditions read this stretch as the Chronicler turning from the world’s families to Israel, and then narrowing toward Judah’s royal line, without allegory and without forcing the parallel lists into one form.

verses.text: and Jesse became the father of his firstborn Eliab, Abinadab the second, Shimea the third,
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesse’s sons begin: “his firstborn Eliab, Abinadab the second, Shimea the third,” The naming is by birth order. 1 Samuel 16–17 also names Eliab and Abinadab among those who stood before Samuel; spellings and counts of Jesse’s sons are not identical across the books and should not be forced together yet, as the list is still incomplete here.

Arminian readers take the three as real brothers in a recorded order.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also start the Jesse list as history, with the Samuel parallel in view, and wait for the rest of the sons in the next verses.

Both traditions read this stretch as the Chronicler turning from the world’s families to Israel, and then narrowing toward Judah’s royal line, without allegory and without forcing the parallel lists into one form.

verses.text: Nethanel the fourth, Raddai the fifth,
verses.arminianNotes:
The list continues: “Nethanel the fourth, Raddai the fifth,” Two more sons are numbered, still toward David, who will be the seventh in the next verse.

Arminian readers keep the numbering as a family record, without inventing stories for names the book does not describe.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same quiet continuation. The Chronicler is counting Jesse’s sons in order, on the way to the royal name.

Both traditions read this stretch as the Chronicler turning from the world’s families to Israel, and then narrowing toward Judah’s royal line, without allegory and without forcing the parallel lists into one form.

verses.text: Ozem the sixth, and David the seventh;
verses.arminianNotes:
The sons close: “Ozem the sixth, and David the seventh;” In this list David is the seventh son of Jesse. 1 Samuel 16–17 presents David among Jesse’s sons in a way that has often been counted differently. The difference should be named and left standing, not harmonized by a theory the present verse does not give.

Arminian readers take “David the seventh” as this book’s own count, a historical claim in this genealogy.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise refuse to invent a missing brother or a revised count in order to make Samuel and this verse identical. The Chronicler places David at the seventh place in Jesse’s house, and that is the royal goal of this unit.

Both traditions read this stretch as the Chronicler turning from the world’s families to Israel, and then narrowing toward Judah’s royal line, without allegory and without forcing the parallel lists into one form.

verses.text: and their sisters were Zeruiah and Abigail. The sons of Zeruiah: Abishai, Joab, and Asahel, three.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesse’s daughters are named: Zeruiah and Abigail. Zeruiah’s sons are Abishai, Joab, and Asahel, three. These are the same three already known from 1–2 Samuel, including the hard history around Joab and Asahel. The genealogy states the kinship without retelling those wars.

Arminian readers take the family facts as real: David’s sister is mother to these three, whose later choices remain their own in the earlier books.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same Samuel background, now reduced to a list. The royal house includes this fierce branch, recorded rather than explained here.

Both traditions read this stretch as the Chronicler turning from the world’s families to Israel, and then narrowing toward Judah’s royal line, without allegory and without forcing the parallel lists into one form.

verses.text: Abigail bore Amasa; and the father of Amasa was Jether the Ishmaelite.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Abigail bore Amasa; and the father of Amasa was Jether the Ishmaelite.” Amasa, who appears in 2 Samuel, is thus David’s nephew through Abigail. Other texts describe Amasa’s father with a different form of the name or a different gentilic; those differences should be named only with care and not forced into one official identification here.

Arminian readers keep the verse as this book’s own statement of the birth.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also decline a forced harmony with every parallel wording. The Chronicler records Amasa’s mother and his father Jether the Ishmaelite, and so closes this first Judah-to-David unit.

Both traditions read this stretch as the Chronicler turning from the world’s families to Israel, and then narrowing toward Judah’s royal line, without allegory and without forcing the parallel lists into one form.
